text: That night: Holmes throws the noose round the reptile's neck

text: That night: Holmes throws the reptile into the iron safe
why: ¶246 states that he threw it into the iron safe.

text: That night: Holmes closes the safe upon the reptile

text: How was the snake got from the safe to the bed and back?
why: The safe is the snake's den, and the ventilator, rope, clamped bed and the snake's return to Roylott's room make this a natural open question.

text: How was the snake got from the safe to the bed and back? — it was trained to come back to the whistle, for the milk
id: q.how_snake_worked=it was trained to come back to the whistle, for the milk
why: The whistle, the saucer of milk on the safe and the snake's den in the safe give a reader reason to consider this; it is offered only as a possibility.

text: How was the snake got from the safe to the bed and back? — he put it up to the ventilator by hand, with the noose on the lash
id: q.how_snake_worked=he put it up to the ventilator by hand, with the noose on the lash
why: The ventilator, the chair Holmes examined and the noose just shown to catch the snake make this a reasonable possibility.

text: How was the snake got from the safe to the bed and back? — it was left to find its own way down the rope
id: q.how_snake_worked=it was left to find its own way down the rope
why: The dummy rope hangs from beside the ventilator down to the bed, so a reader can consider this.

text: What made the clanging sound? — the snake's den is the iron safe, and its door shuts on it
why: ¶245-246 call the safe the creature's den and show its door closed on it; linking an iron door to the metallic clang of ¶50 is an obvious inference.

text: What is the small dog lash tied into a loop for? — with the noose a snake can be caught by the neck and carried at arm's length
why: ¶246 shows Holmes using the noose to catch the snake by the neck and carry it at arm's length.
